ticket.created: Emit After the Write →

A Shared Emitter and Event Registry

events/emitter.js: one EventEmitter every service and listener imports, plus a single source of truth for event-name strings.

// Figure 5.1: the shared bus and its event-name registry (src/events/emitter.js)
import { EventEmitter } from 'node:events';

const domainEvents = new EventEmitter();

export default domainEvents;

export const EVENTS = {
  TICKET_CREATED: 'ticket.created',
  TICKET_ASSIGNED: 'ticket.assigned',
  TICKET_COMMENTED: 'ticket.commented',
  TICKET_STATUS_CHANGED: 'ticket.status_changed',
};

domainEvents is created exactly once, here, and exported as a default export. Every other file that wants to emit or listen for a domain event imports this same instance — import domainEvents from '../events/emitter.js' — rather than constructing its own new EventEmitter(). That's the same import-as-singleton idiom config/db.js's PrismaClient already relies on: a module in Node only ever runs once no matter how many files import it, so the object it exports is automatically shared by everyone who imports it — no separate dependency-injection container needed to guarantee that.

EVENTS solves a smaller but easy-to-get-wrong problem: .on() and .emit() both take the event name as a plain string, and EventEmitter has no way to check that a string used in one file matches a string used in another — 'ticket.created' and 'ticket_created' would silently just be two different events, one with no listeners. Writing EVENTS.TICKET_CREATED everywhere instead turns that class of typo into an undefined-is-not-a-valid- event-name bug or an import error, not a listener that quietly never fires.
